title: Families, failures and a fix: why inquests often don't stop repeat deaths
label: 3 November 2026 · Learning from Inquests
summary: Bereaved family members gave stark examples of inquests that failed to bring change: late disclosure, unequal access to legal help, and prevention of future deaths (PFD) reports that rarely produce enforcement. Experts from INQUEST and the Preventable Deaths Tracker explained that PFDs are a tiny fraction of all inquests, responses are inconsistent, and there is no national system to collect, analyse and follow up inquest findings. They recommended a digital national inquest database and an independent oversight body to spot trends, force follow-up and report to Parliament.

glossary.definition: A public fact-finding hearing led by a coroner to establish who died, when, where and how.
Prevention of Future Deaths report: a coroner’s recommendation to prevent similar deaths in future.
The judicial officer who investigates sudden or unexplained deaths and may hold an inquest.
An inquest required where the state may bear responsibility for a death (higher duty to investigate).
Care Quality Commission, the health and social care regulator for England.
Prison suicide prevention process (Assessment, Care in Custody and Teamwork).
A proposed change to allow early legal funding for families in some inquests involving public bodies.

chapters.title: How inquests felt to families
chapters.takeaway: Families described inquests as retraumatising, unequal and often powerless to trigger real change.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We asked witnesses with lived experience to explain why the coronial follow-up system needs to change.

turns.speaker: Johnny Santer
turns.text: My son Gabriel died falling from a multi-storey car park in 2020. The inquest process was chaotic: I didn’t get the coroner’s bundle until the night before, and I had no lawyer then.

turns.speaker: Richard Caseby
turns.text: My son Matthew died after escaping a private mental health unit and being struck by a train. I had to use my investigative background to uncover evidence and then rely on legal aid to get representation.

turns.speaker: Dr Kate Szymankiewicz
turns.text: Our daughter Ruth died in a privately run NHS-commissioned eating-disorder unit. The jury found unlawful killing, yet the coroner declined to issue a PFD and nothing meaningful changed.

turns.speaker: Tessa Munt
turns.text: Did you have realistic expectations about what an inquest could do before you started?

turns.speaker: Johnny Santer
turns.text: I knew the basic questions a coroner asks, but not how to turn an inquest into prevention. Representation makes a huge difference: after I saw a barrister get a PFD in a similar case, I realised what could be done.

turns.speaker: Richard Caseby
turns.text: I underestimated how adversarial inquests can be. Public bodies turn up with teams of lawyers funded by the state. Families are expected to be ‘at the heart’ but often are not.

turns.speaker: Dr Kate Szymankiewicz
turns.text: We only found INQUEST by chance; without that help we wouldn't have known to seek legal aid. The coroner initially seemed focused on narrow outcomes and not the systemic issues we wanted explored.

chapters.title: Prevention of Future Deaths reports: rare and limited
chapters.takeaway: PFDs cover only a tiny share of inquests, coroners have wide discretion, and PFDs lack enforcement and consistent follow-up.

turns.speaker: Vikki Slade
turns.text: Only Richard’s case got a PFD. How useful was it, and why is enforcement a problem?

turns.speaker: Richard Caseby
turns.text: The PFD highlighted fence height, record-keeping and risk-assessment failures. It helped: the Priory later raised fences and was prosecuted. But I could push because of my resources; many families can't.

turns.speaker: Johnny Santer
turns.text: Gabriel’s death did not get a PFD. There are many virtually identical multi-storey car park deaths—Georgia’s tracker shows dozens—but no consistent action from operators like Q-Park.

turns.speaker: Dr Kate Szymankiewicz
turns.text: Even when juries find unlawful killing and list systemic failures, coroners sometimes decline PFDs after providers promise fixes; but there is often no checking that promises are kept.

turns.speaker: Dr Georgia Richards
turns.text: PFDs are issued in about 1.7% of inquests. Coroners decide whether to write one; courts confirmed that discretion in a 2022 legal case. That creates big geographic variation.

turns.speaker: Deborah Coles
turns.text: PFDs can matter—there are successful campaigns such as Awaab’s law and Seni’s law—but many reports are formulaic, and organisations treat them as reputation-management rather than a safety duty.

turns.speaker: Warinder Juss
turns.text: Would coroners be required to issue PFDs where culpability is found?

turns.speaker: Dr Georgia Richards
turns.text: No statutory threshold forces a PFD. The coroner’s discretion, uneven practice and lack of enforcement mean many important lessons are never captured or acted on.

chapters.title: Data and oversight gaps
chapters.takeaway: There is no national database of all inquests; that prevents systematic analysis, trend-spotting and timely action.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What follow-up systems already exist and what is missing?

turns.speaker: Dr Georgia Richards
turns.text: There’s no single statutory database of all inquests. My Preventable Deaths Tracker collects every PFD since 2013 and tracks responses, but it’s privately funded and not a substitute for a national system.

turns.speaker: Dr Georgia Richards
turns.text: We found that responses improved from under a third to about two-thirds after the chief coroner started publishing non-response lists. For 2024 some reports show 92% with responses published—but publication rules and templates are now changing in ways that risk reversing progress.

turns.speaker: Deborah Coles
turns.text: Without a national system, narrative conclusions—where juries describe systemic failures—are lost unless highlighted by charities or families. There is no routine follow-up to check whether recommended changes happen on the ground.

turns.speaker: Tony Vaughan
turns.text: What models exist abroad?

turns.speaker: Dr Georgia Richards
turns.text: Australia, Canada and others have national coronial databases. Australia’s system grew after a royal commission into deaths in custody. These systems enable trend analysis and policy response; we could adopt a similar statutory database.

turns.speaker: Mrs Russell
turns.text: Is your tracker public?

turns.speaker: Dr Georgia Richards
turns.text: Yes, but it has limited funding, and some content sits behind a paywall because there was no Government funding after the Committee’s 2024 evidence session. We need a publicly funded digital system.

turns.speaker: Deborah Coles
turns.text: A national oversight mechanism (NOM) would need the database to feed it: collect recommendations and inquest findings, analyse themes, and crucially follow up with powers to require information and work with regulators.

chapters.title: Practical reforms families and experts want
chapters.takeaway: Proposals include a national database, an independent oversight body to follow up recommendations, early legal funding, digitalisation and clearer coroner guidance.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: If you could give Government one message about improving learning from inquests, what would it be?

turns.speaker: Dr Kate Szymankiewicz
turns.text: Keep the human cost front and centre: create an oversight mechanism that actually makes change happen and brings Ministers from relevant Departments together.

turns.speaker: Johnny Santer
turns.text: Families just want lessons learned so others don’t die the same way. If private companies face no real consequence they won’t act—there needs to be power and accountability.

turns.speaker: Richard Caseby
turns.text: End the cliff-edge after PFDs: appoint a commissioner for prevention of future deaths with a small secretariat to spot recurring failings and hold organisations to account.

turns.speaker: Deborah Coles
turns.text: The NOM should be independent, able to request information, follow up implementation, and report to Parliament. Families must be part of its governance so lived experience shapes priorities.

turns.speaker: Dr Georgia Richards
turns.text: Digitalise and publish in real time: a statutory national database of all inquests is the foundation. With live dashboards you can spot trends quickly and evaluate policies such as Hillsborough Law.

turns.speaker: Tessa Munt
turns.text: What about legal representation?

turns.speaker: Deborah Coles
turns.text: Early access to legal aid saves families retraumatisation and improves scrutiny. The trigger point for funding should be earlier than now so families get advice before pre-inquest hearings.

turns.speaker: Dr Georgia Richards
turns.text: And evaluate policies: a national database lets you measure whether changes actually reduce similar deaths rather than just producing a report that gathers dust.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: That concludes the session. Thank you all for your courage and for your practical proposals.

turns.speaker: Deborah Coles
turns.text: Please act. Families have campaigned for decades; an independent mechanism would finally make learning from deaths consistent, transparent and accountable.

turns.speaker: Dr Georgia Richards
turns.text: We already have tools and international examples. With modest investment we can stop this being a postcode lottery and save lives.
